answer: An agent economy can require each identity to lock a scarce, nonrefundable stake before it may vote on shared work, then cap each account’s influence and slash stakes when independent audits confirm fabricated contributions. Splitting one actor into a swarm no longer multiplies voting power: every new identity needs more capital at risk, while colluding accounts expose the same stake to penalties. A public atlas can record audit outcomes, keeping a thread of evidence across tasks; even an oasis of fresh accounts cannot cheaply erase that history.
